areas.name: Palo Seco

why_here: Nature attraction score 62/100 — top-tier natural draw at national screening scale.
Attraction exceeds tourism supply by 44 points — a measured development gap.

Resilience function 71/100 — ecosystems here sit between hazard and people or between slope and settlement.

About 61,000 people live inside the area — a local labour and enterprise base.
The area intersects an indigenous comarca; any tourism development must be community-led.
areas.natural_assets: The area's natural asset base comprises shallow shelf under 20 m (186 km²), forest cover over 88% of the area, 900 m of local relief, rising to 2378 m and 4 mapped beaches. It overlaps the protected area(s) Fortuna, La Amistad y Palo Seco, Palo Seco, San San Pond Sak, covering 70% of the area. Named features mapped here include Oreba Chocolate Tour, Boca del Drago, Cangilones de Mague, Balneario Piedra Caliza, Finca Cerro Azul and Quijada del Diablo. It sits predominantly in the Talamancan montane forests ecoregion, draining the Río Changuinola basin.
areas.tourism_context: OpenStreetMap records 17 accommodation points, 27 food-service points, 5 attractions, 18 named trails, 0 dive/surf operators and 6 marinas or ferry points. Modelled travel time to the nearest tourism gateway is 6.7 hours; the accessibility score is 27/100. OSM density under-records places that receive few visitors, so a low count here is partly a symptom of low development rather than an independent measure of it.
areas.biodiversity: A mean of 353 vertebrate species have been recorded per screening cell here, in the Talamancan montane forests ecoregion. 70% of the area carries protected status and under 1% is in a strict IUCN category. Biodiversity value scores 59/100 and the protection gap 74/100.
areas.resilience: Coastal ecosystems here — shallow shelf under 20 m (186 km²) — sit between open water and low-lying settlement and tourism assets. On the screening assumption that intact mangrove and reef attenuate wave energy and stabilise shorelines, the area scores 71/100 for resilience function. This is a spatial coincidence of ecosystem and exposure, not a modelled reduction in flood damage.
conservation_action: Assess the case for new or extended marine protection over the reef–mangrove complex, including whether an existing coastal management category could be upgraded rather than a new area declared.
Where mangrove has been cleared, target replanting at the landward margin and restore tidal connectivity before considering any engineered shoreline works.
Consolidate forest protection on upper slopes and restore degraded margins, prioritising continuity with existing protected land rather than isolated patches.
Review management effectiveness of the existing designation: much of this area carries a permissive category that may not hold the values identified here.
tourism_investment: No site inside this area currently meets the screening test for visitor infrastructure (road access within 2.5 km, a settlement within 12 km, and outside a strict protection core). The case here is conservation-led.
nature_investment: **Protect forest** — about 259,406 ha across 2,756 km2. Intact forest on slopes above settlements and visitor infrastructure; retaining cover is the low-cost option and it is also the attraction.
**Protect reef and shallow shelf** — about 17,226 ha across 255 km2. Shallow reef-capable habitat with little strict protection, in an area where snorkelling and diving are or could be the product.
**Protect wetland** — about 1,970 ha across 255 km2. Herbaceous wetland with water-regulation and birdlife value that is itself a visitor product.

**Restore mangrove** — about 35 ha across 548 km2. Mangrove is thin or fragmented here but the coastal setting supports it and there are people and tourism assets behind it; replanting at the landward margin and restoring tidal flow is indicated.

In total: roughly 278,602 ha to hold under better protection and 35 ha to restore. Protecting functioning ecosystems is cheaper and more certain than recreating them, so the protection actions should be sequenced first.
areas.jobs: An indicative package here - 35 ha of restoration and 278,602 ha brought under active management - would support roughly **110-340 direct jobs**, or **190-810 including indirect and induced** employment. About 61,000 people live inside the area. The plausible channels are dive and snorkel guiding, boat operation and equipment servicing, nature and birding guiding, trail construction and maintenance, beach services, food and beverage, and small accommodation and protected-area management, ranger and interpretation roles.
areas.jobs_caveat: These are order-of-magnitude figures for a hypothetical package, not a forecast. They assume finance, tenure, skills and visitor demand that this screening cannot observe, and restoration employment is expressed as full-time equivalents while a 5-year programme runs, not permanent posts. Because the area intersects an indigenous comarca, the master plan's own requirement applies: development must be community-led, with free prior and informed consent and equitable, durable benefit sharing.
risks: Access at 6.7 hours from a gateway may cap realistic demand; improving access will itself increase pressure.
Land tenure and governance in comarca territory require a distinct process; conventional concession models may not apply.
Most of the area is already designated; the binding constraint may be management capacity and enforcement rather than legal status.
OSM-derived supply counts and GBIF-derived richness both carry recording bias; both should be validated locally before investment decisions.
further_analysis: Ground-truthing of tourism supply and visitor numbers, which no open dataset records reliably at this scale.
Reef condition and mangrove health assessment — extent is mapped here, condition is not.
Coastal hazard overlay once the ~90 m flood hazard layers are available, to convert the resilience proxy into an exposure-based estimate.
Catchment hydrology and erosion assessment to test the assumed watershed-protection benefit.
Ecological, social, legal and stakeholder assessment before any protected-area designation or boundary change is proposed. Nothing here constitutes a designation recommendation.

why_here: Nature attraction score 66/100 — top-tier natural draw at national screening scale.
Attraction exceeds tourism supply by 24 points — a measured development gap.
Biodiversity value 61/100, with a mean of 511 vertebrate species recorded per screening cell.
Resilience function 92/100 — ecosystems here sit between hazard and people or between slope and settlement.
Modelled travel time to the nearest tourism gateway is 2.9 hours.
About 7,100 people live inside the area — a local labour and enterprise base.
areas.natural_assets: The area's natural asset base comprises forest cover over 96% of the area. It overlaps the protected area(s) Chagres, covering 88% of the area. Named features mapped here include Sendero a río las cascadas, Mirador, Mirador Cerro Pelado, Cascada Romeo, Cascada Julieta and Cerro Jefe. It sits predominantly in the Isthmian-Atlantic moist forests ecoregion, draining the Canal de Panamá basin.
areas.tourism_context: OpenStreetMap records 3 accommodation points, 3 food-service points, 1 attractions, 1 named trails, 0 dive/surf operators and 0 marinas or ferry points. Modelled travel time to the nearest tourism gateway is 2.9 hours; the accessibility score is 66/100. OSM density under-records places that receive few visitors, so a low count here is partly a symptom of low development rather than an independent measure of it.
areas.biodiversity: A mean of 511 vertebrate species have been recorded per screening cell here, in the Isthmian-Atlantic moist forests ecoregion. 88% of the area carries protected status and 86% is in a strict IUCN category. Biodiversity value scores 61/100 and the protection gap 14/100.
areas.resilience: Forest covers 96% of the area across 601 m of local relief in the Canal de Panamá basin. Maintaining that cover on slopes plausibly supports infiltration, limits erosion and moderates runoff reaching downstream settlements and tourism infrastructure. Resilience score 92/100. No hydrological modelling has been undertaken.
conservation_action: Consolidate forest protection on upper slopes and restore degraded margins, prioritising continuity with existing protected land rather than isolated patches.
tourism_investment: No site inside this area currently meets the screening test for visitor infrastructure (road access within 2.5 km, a settlement within 12 km, and outside a strict protection core). The case here is conservation-led.
Direct new construction to already-developed settlements at the periphery, and invest in the management capacity - rangers, monitoring, permitting - that a rising visitor trend will require.
nature_investment: **Protect forest** — about 17,367 ha across 180 km2. Intact forest on slopes above settlements and visitor infrastructure; retaining cover is the low-cost option and it is also the attraction.

In total: roughly 17,367 ha to hold under better protection and 0 ha to restore. Protecting functioning ecosystems is cheaper and more certain than recreating them, so the protection actions should be sequenced first.
areas.jobs: An indicative package here - 17,367 ha brought under active management - would support roughly **5-20 direct jobs**, or **10-50 including indirect and induced** employment. About 7,100 people live inside the area. The plausible channels are nature and birding guiding, trail construction and maintenance, protected-area management, ranger and interpretation roles and local food supply, crafts and transport into the visitor economy.
areas.jobs_caveat: These are order-of-magnitude figures for a hypothetical package, not a forecast. They assume finance, tenure, skills and visitor demand that this screening cannot observe, and restoration employment is expressed as full-time equivalents while a 5-year programme runs, not permanent posts.
risks: High ecological sensitivity (71/100). Carrying capacity should be set before, not after, demand grows.
Most of the area is already designated; the binding constraint may be management capacity and enforcement rather than legal status.
OSM-derived supply counts and GBIF-derived richness both carry recording bias; both should be validated locally before investment decisions.
further_analysis: Ground-truthing of tourism supply and visitor numbers, which no open dataset records reliably at this scale.
Catchment hydrology and erosion assessment to test the assumed watershed-protection benefit.
Ecological, social, legal and stakeholder assessment before any protected-area designation or boundary change is proposed. Nothing here constitutes a designation recommendation.
Consultation with ATP, MiAmbiente and the relevant Comité de Gestión de Destino.
areas.gov_alignment: This area lies within the government's priority destination “Ciudad de Panama - Taboga” (100% of the area), so the findings here speak to a destination the Plan Maestro 2025-2030 has already committed to.

why_here: Nature attraction score 63/100 — top-tier natural draw at national screening scale.
Biodiversity value 63/100, with a mean of 418 vertebrate species recorded per screening cell.
Protection gap 81/100: 38% of the area has some protected status but only 0% is in a strict IUCN category (I–IV).
Resilience function 79/100 — ecosystems here sit between hazard and people or between slope and settlement.
Mangrove covers 39 km² (27% of the area).
31% of the area is shallow shelf under 20 m — reef and seagrass-capable habitat.
Modelled travel time to the nearest tourism gateway is 1.0 hours.
About 9,900 people live inside the area — a local labour and enterprise base.

It overlaps the protected area(s) Bahía de Chame, covering 38% of the area. Named features mapped here include Mirador Cerro Chame, Cerro de la Zona, Cerro Guasimo, Cerro Botija and Cerro Campanita. It sits predominantly in the South American Pacific mangroves ecoregion, draining the Ríos entre el Antón y el Caimito basin.

areas.resilience: Coastal ecosystems here — mangrove (39 km²) and shallow shelf under 20 m (46 km²) — sit between open water and low-lying settlement and tourism assets. On the screening assumption that intact mangrove and reef attenuate wave energy and stabilise shorelines, the area scores 79/100 for resilience function. This is a spatial coincidence of ecosystem and exposure, not a modelled reduction in flood damage.
conservation_action: Assess the case for new or extended marine protection over the reef–mangrove complex, including whether an existing coastal management category could be upgraded rather than a new area declared.
Where mangrove has been cleared, target replanting at the landward margin and restore tidal connectivity before considering any engineered shoreline works.
Review management effectiveness of the existing designation: much of this area carries a permissive category that may not hold the values identified here.
tourism_investment: No site inside this area currently meets the screening test for visitor infrastructure (road access within 2.5 km, a settlement within 12 km, and outside a strict protection core). The case here is conservation-led.
Direct new construction to already-developed settlements at the periphery, and invest in the management capacity - rangers, monitoring, permitting - that a rising visitor trend will require.
nature_investment: **Protect reef and shallow shelf** — about 4,130 ha across 74 km2. Shallow reef-capable habitat with little strict protection, in an area where snorkelling and diving are or could be the product.

**Protect mangrove** — about 3,532 ha across 110 km2. Mangrove is present and functioning between open water and low-lying assets; protecting standing mangrove is cheaper and more certain than replanting it.

In total: roughly 7,662 ha to hold under better protection and 0 ha to restore. Protecting functioning ecosystems is cheaper and more certain than recreating them, so the protection actions should be sequenced first.

About 9,900 people live inside the area. The plausible channels are dive and snorkel guiding, boat operation and equipment servicing, kayak and boat tours, and paid mangrove restoration crews, beach services, food and beverage, and small accommodation and protected-area management, ranger and interpretation roles.
areas.jobs_caveat: These are order-of-magnitude figures for a hypothetical package, not a forecast.
